introduction: In these readings Bahá’u’lláh speaks with the voice of God. 'Verily I am God; no God is there but Me', the text says, and it identifies the speaker with the one who spoke to Moses on Sinai; and the same pages say 'I speak not of Mine own desire', 'I am but a servant of God', and describe a human temple through whose tongue another speaks. Many passages are in that voice addressing individuals: 'We have heard thy call'. A hundred of the guide's three hundred quotations are read here, ten from each tenth of the reading order, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the bush that says 'I am God' in the Qur'an and in Exodus, Isaiah's oracles in the first person, 'before Abraham was, I am', 'he that hath seen me hath seen the Father', Krishna in the Gita, Wisdom speaking in Proverbs, and with them the disclaimers, 'my doctrine is not mine', 'I can of mine own self do nothing'. Nine push back or add a side, since the claim is as strong as any a religion makes: Herod acclaimed with 'the voice of a god', Ezekiel's prince who said 'I am a God', Isaiah's 'my glory will I not give to another', the Qur'an's ban on any prophet saying 'be slaves of me', Hallaj, Emerson and Whitman finding the divine 'I' in everyone, Feuerbach, and the angel who told John 'see thou do it not'.
questions: The same speaker says 'Verily I am God' and 'I am but a servant of God'. How do the readings ask us to hear the two together?
The Qur'an and Exodus have a bush say 'I am God'. How does that help in understanding a human being through whom such words come?
Ezekiel's prince and Herod were condemned for a claim that sounds similar. What, according to the readings, is the difference?
Emerson and Whitman found the divine 'I' in every person. Is that what these readings mean?
Many passages say 'We have heard thy call' to someone by name. What would it be to receive such a letter?
What would count, for you, as evidence that a voice of this kind is what it says it is?

outside.why: The Qur'an gives the words that came to Moses from the bush: lo, I, even I, am God; there is no God save me.
The Apocalypse has a voice say: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending.
Jesus said: I have not spoken of myself; the Father which sent me gave me a commandment what I should say.
The Qur'an says of its Prophet's speech that it is naught save an inspiration that is inspired.
Israel's confession is the same sentence: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.
Exodus tells who spoke on Sinai: a voice out of a bush that burned and was not consumed.
Acts tells of a king whom the crowd acclaimed with 'the voice of a god, and not of a man', and who fell because he gave not God the glory. What marks the difference the readings claim?
Jesus said: my doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me.
Jesus said: I can of mine own self do nothing; I seek not mine own will, but the will of the Father.
Paul says of Christ that, being in the form of God, he took upon him the form of a servant.
The Qur'an says that those who swear allegiance to the Prophet swear allegiance only to God.
Peter writes that prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men spake as they were moved.
Israel said at Horeb: we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire.
Amos asks: the lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord God hath spoken, who can but prophesy?
Malachi promises that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
Jesus said he spoke in parables because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
Accused of making himself God, Jesus answered from the Psalms: is it not written, I said, ye are gods?
Jesus said: I and my Father are one; and they took up stones to stone him.
Hallaj said: I am he whom I love, and he whom I love is I. He was put to death for such words. How do the readings distinguish their claim from his?
The Qur'an tells of a letter that opens: in the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful.
Jesus said to Philip: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
Isaiah hears: I am the Lord, that is my name, and my glory will I not give to another. How do the readings understand a human voice saying 'I am God' without transgressing that?
Paul speaks of the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
God names himself to Moses in the first person and nothing more: I AM THAT I AM.
Jesus said to those who challenged his age: before Abraham was, I am.
The Qur'an says no man given the Scripture and the prophethood could tell people 'be slaves of me instead of God'. What is the 'I' that speaks in this reading?

Emerson heard Jesus say in a jubilee of sublime emotion 'I am divine; through me, God acts', and thought the same true of every person. Is the voice in these readings one that anyone could find within?
Krishna says in the Gita: when righteousness declines, I rise from age to age and take visible shape.
In Proverbs Wisdom speaks in her own person: I was set up from everlasting, before the earth was.
Paul speaks of one who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
Paul asks: know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?
John's Gospel says that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
Isaiah's lips were touched with a live coal before he could speak for God.
Moses was told, when he pleaded a slow tongue: who hath made man's mouth? I will be with thy mouth.
Jesus promised his followers a mouth and wisdom which their adversaries could not gainsay.
Feuerbach argued that the true sense of theology is anthropology, and the divine predicates are human ones. When a human temple is addressed as the tongue of God, who is speaking?
Solomon asked: the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house?
The disciples asked of Jesus: what manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
Jesus spoke of living water that becomes a well springing up into everlasting life.
Matthew says that on the mountain his face did shine as the sun.
A psalmist says: while I was musing the fire burned; then spake I with my tongue.
A psalm calls on sun and moon to praise the Lord, for he commanded and they were created.
Krishna says in the Gita: all these hang on me, as a row of pearls upon its string.
Whitman wrote: divine am I inside and out, and I make holy whatever I touch. What separates a prophet's 'I' from a poet's?
John's Gospel begins: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.
Hebrews speaks of the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person.
A psalm says: by the word of the Lord were the heavens made.
Matthew says he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
A psalm says: the entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
The officers sent to arrest Jesus came back saying: never man spake like this man.
Hebrews says of Christ that he was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
John says he came unto his own, and his own received him not; but some received him.
Jesus told his disciples: blessed are your ears, for they hear what prophets desired to hear.
Jesus asked his disciples what people said of him, and then: but whom say ye that I am?
Thomas, who had doubted, was convinced at last and said: my Lord and my God.
Simeon, who had waited long, said in the temple: mine eyes have seen thy salvation.
The Qur'an recalls a primordial question put to all souls: am I not your Lord? They said: yea, verily.
Moses was told at the bush: put off thy shoes, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
The angel said: fear not; behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy.
John saw a great white throne, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away.
John wrote his book from an island of banishment, 'for the word of God'.
Paul writes that he suffers unto bonds, but the word of God is not bound.
Jesus said: the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Lovelace held that stone walls do not a prison make for a soul that is free.
Isaiah says: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Zephaniah says: the great day of the Lord is near, it is near, and hasteth greatly.
Isaiah's servant is despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows.
Paul writes from confinement under the title he chose: I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord.
Jesus said in the garden: my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.
Jesus told Nathanael: before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.
A psalmist says to God: thou understandest my thought afar off; such knowledge is too wonderful for me.
Jeremiah hears God say to his people: I have loved thee with an everlasting love.
Isaiah hears: I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.
God tells Moses: I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and have heard their cry.
Isaiah hears: before they call, I will answer; and while they are yet speaking, I will hear.
In the Qur'an God says: I am nigh; I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto me.
Genesis says that God heard the voice of the lad where he was.
Matthew's Gospel ends: lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world.
When John fell at the feet of the one who spoke to him, he was told: see thou do it not; I am thy fellowservant; worship God. Who is it that says 'We have heard thy call'?
Isaiah says: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings.
Malachi says a book of remembrance was written for them that feared the Lord.
John's first letter says: that which we have seen and heard declare we unto you.
Acts says that on the day of Pentecost a sound came from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind.
James says: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only.
Paul closes a long letter with greetings by name to those who had helped him.
The Qur'an says: God is the light of the heavens and the earth.
The Song of Songs announces: the winter is past; the time of the singing of birds is come.
A psalm says: this is the day which the Lord hath made.
The Qur'an likens a goodly word to a goodly tree, its root firm, its branches in heaven.
John's first letter says the world passeth away, but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
The first of the commandments says the same: thou shalt have no other gods before me.
In the Qur'an Jacob regains his sight when Joseph's garment is laid on his face.
A psalm praises the one who sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Paul's rule was to pray without ceasing, and in every thing give thanks.
Isaiah hears: I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass.
The Qur'an says: he will not be questioned as to that which he doeth.
A psalmist asks: whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?
Ezekiel is sent to a prince who said 'I am a God': yet thou art a man, and not God. By what do the readings ask to be told apart from him?
Ephesians calls: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.

ezekiel-thou-art-a-man-and-not-god.text: Son of man, say unto the prince of Tyrus, Thus saith the Lord God; Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God, I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the seas; yet thou art a man, and not God, though thou set thine heart as the heart of God

exodus-i-have-heard-their-cry.text: And the Lord said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows

john-under-the-fig-tree.text: Nathanael saith unto him, Whence knowest thou me? Jesus answered and said unto him, Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee

isaiah-i-am-the-lord-and-there-is-none-e.text: I am the Lord, and there is none else

genesis-god-heard-the-voice-of-the-lad.text: And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is
